questions.q: What does superdense coding allow Alice to send Bob, and with what resources?
options: An unlimited number of classical bits using a single pre-shared entangled pair
2 classical bits, by transmitting only 1 qubit, after consuming 1 pre-shared entangled pair
1 classical bit, which is no better than what an unentangled qubit transmission could achieve
2 qubits of quantum information, using only 1 classical bit
questions.explain: Superdense coding's whole point is beating the ordinary 1-classical-bit-per-qubit limit: with 1 pre-shared entangled pair as fuel, Alice sends 2 classical bits using only 1 physically transmitted qubit.

questions.q: To send the message '11', Alice applies Z then X to her half of the shared |Φ+⟩ pair. What is the resulting shared state, and how does it compare to the other three possible messages' results?
options: The result is a classical probability mixture, not a quantum state
The result depends on what Bob does, not just on Alice's operation
The result is (|01⟩−|10⟩)/√2, and it is mutually orthogonal to the other three possible results (unchanged |Φ+⟩, X-applied |Ψ+⟩, and Z-applied |Φ−⟩)
The result is identical to |Φ+⟩, making '11' indistinguishable from '00'
questions.explain: The four possible operations {I,X,Z,ZX} applied to Alice's half of |Φ+⟩ produce the four mutually orthogonal Bell states (verified by direct computation), which is exactly what lets Bob distinguish all four cases perfectly.

questions.q: Why can Bob determine Alice's full 2-bit message with certainty, using only one Bell-basis measurement on the two qubits he ends up holding?
options: Bob must perform four separate measurements, one for each possible message
The four possible resulting states are mutually orthogonal, so a single measurement in the Bell basis can distinguish between all four with zero ambiguity
Bob can read Alice's mind about which operation she applied, without needing any measurement
Bob's result is only correct 50% of the time; the rest is guesswork
questions.explain: Mutual orthogonality between the four possible results is exactly what makes a single, unambiguous measurement possible -- if the states overlapped at all, the measurement could sometimes misidentify which operation Alice applied.

questions.q: In what precise sense are superdense coding and quantum teleportation described as 'dual' protocols?
options: Teleportation sends 1 qubit of quantum information using 2 classical bits plus 1 shared entangled pair, while superdense coding sends 2 classical bits using 1 transmitted qubit plus 1 shared entangled pair -- the resource roles are swapped
They are identical protocols with different names
Superdense coding is simply teleportation run backward in time
Teleportation requires no entanglement, while superdense coding requires two entangled pairs
questions.explain: Both protocols spend exactly one pre-shared entangled pair, but trade different communication resources: teleportation trades classical bits for quantum state transfer, while superdense coding trades entanglement for extra classical capacity per transmitted qubit.

questions.q: What does superdense coding demonstrate about entanglement as a resource?
options: Entanglement makes classical communication entirely unnecessary
Entanglement only matters for computation, never for communication
Entanglement is a genuine, quantifiable communication resource that can be 'spent' to exceed limits that would otherwise apply to an unentangled qubit transmission
Entanglement has no practical use beyond demonstrating correlations in physics experiments
questions.explain: Superdense coding concretely shows that pre-distributed entanglement, treated as a consumable resource, lets a protocol beat the classical-information limit of a single qubit transmission -- entanglement is doing real, quantifiable work, not just sitting there as a correlation.
